newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus president backs economic plan to 2000.
newsitem.headline: Belarus president backs economic plan to 2000.

text.p: Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, who favours a state-dominated economy, has approved a plan to the year 2000 foreseeing gradual falls in inflation, higher output and better wages.
No comment was available from Western analysts on Wednesday on the 500-page document, which was approved the day before at a meeting of Lukashenko, his advisers and regional leaders.
A diplomatic source said analysts were still studying the plan and it was too soon to draw any conclusions from it.
The plan forecasts monthly inflation falling from roughly three percent currently to 2.5 percent by the end of the year, two percent in 1997 and 0.5 to 1.5 percent from 1998-2000.
The document also pledged to have the Belarussian rouble fall against the dollar in line with inflation.

Lukashenko told the meeting in remarks broadcast by radio that there would "no hard currency corridors" -- an inflation-busting move implemented for six months in July to hold the rouble rate between 13,100 and 15,500 to the dollar.
The International Monetary Fund, which suspended credits to the country of 10 million people in March, recommended in May that Belarus devalue its rouble by 20 percent and establish a floating rate.
The Zvyazda newspaper on Wednesday quoted the central bank as saying the rouble would not fall more than 20 percent below the current corridor's lower limit of 15,500 to the dollar.
Lukashenko also said he would allow no further devaluation of the rouble, which stood at 14,550 on Wednesday.

The budget deficit would be three percent of gross domestic product in 1996. It would be allowed to grow to four percent in 1997 and settle at three to four percent from 1998-2000. The deficit was 2.6 percent of GDP last year.
The plan forecast a one precent rise in GDP over 1995 levels, with increases of five percent in 1997 and four to six percent from 1998-2000.
Wages would grow five percent in 1997, then eight to 10 percent and show a "noticeable improvement" by 2000.
Unemployment would stand at 4.5 percent of the workforce by the end of 1996, five percent by the end of 1997, and five to 5.5 percent from 1998-2000. --Kiev Newsroom +380 44 229 2264
